---
title: "D0 Executive summary, inventory and tiering"
---

## Executive summary

The SME Lending Decision Platform scores small-business loan applicants and turns that
score into four decisions: whether to lend, at what price, which booked loans to watch,
and which borrowers to offer more credit. Everything runs on a synthetic book of
{{< var score.n_applicants >}} applicants, of whom {{< var score.n_booked >}} were booked.

**Business Credit Score (D4).** A weight-of-evidence scorecard on
{{< var score.n_features >}} features. On the held-out {{< var score.test_share >}} of
applicants it reaches an AUC of {{< var score.auc_holdout >}} (bootstrap interval
{{< var score.auc_ci_lo >}} to {{< var score.auc_ci_hi >}}) against a committed gate of
{{< var score.gate >}}. On the held-out loans the bank actually books, the same model
scores {{< var score.pop.booked.auc >}}: the gate is met on a population wider than the one
the bank lends to. That is the first of six open findings the chapter raises about itself.

**Loan Adjudication (D5).** A gradient-boosted model on {{< var adj.n_features >}} inputs,
including the score, followed by a policy layer that returns Approve, Refer or Decline
with reasons. Held-out AUC over all applicants is {{< var adj.auc >}} against a gate of
{{< var adj.gate_auc >}}; the decision mix on that population is
{{< var adj.mix.Approve >}} approve, {{< var adj.mix.Refer >}} refer,
{{< var adj.mix.Decline >}} decline.

**Pricing (D6).** A deterministic return-on-equity calculation: given the score's PD and
the market assumptions, it solves for the rate that clears a
{{< var market.roe_hurdle >}} ROE hurdle and flags booked loans quoted below it. It
estimates nothing.

**Early Warning (D7).** A behavioural model over the booked book's monthly history that
places loans in risk tiers and names the triggers that fired. It is gated on how many
deteriorations it captures in its top decile, with AUC reported but not gated, because
noise in the data puts a low ceiling on AUC. Its headline figures arrive with the chapter.

**Line Increase (D8).** A gradient-boosted candidate model plus amount rules and an incremental-ROE test,
which offers more credit only to the lower-risk half of the book. Its headline figures
arrive with the chapter.

## Inventory

| Component | Code | Classification | Estimated parameters | Output consumed by |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Business Credit Score | `score/` | model | WoE bins, logistic coefficients | every other component |
| Loan Adjudication | `adjudication/` | model | gradient-boosted trees; policy cutoffs calibrated at train time | the portal |
| Pricing | `pricing/` | deterministic calculation tool | none | the portal |
| Early Warning | `ews/` | model | gradient-boosted trees; tier cutoffs calibrated at train time | the portal |
| Line Increase | `line_increase/` | model | gradient-boosted trees; offer cutoff calibrated at train time | the portal |

### Why pricing is listed as a tool, not a model

A model, in the sense of SR 11-7 and its successors, turns data into an *estimate*, and its
risk comes from the estimate being wrong. The pricing engine (`pricing/src/engine.py`) has
no estimated parameters. It is arithmetic: interest income less cost of funds, expected
loss, operating cost and tax, divided by allocated capital, solved for the rate that
clears the hurdle. The same inputs always give the same rate.

Its risk lives in two inputs, and each is governed where it belongs:

- **The PD** comes from the Business Credit Score, which is inventoried and tiered as a
  model (D4). A change to the scorecard forces pricing to be re-run (D3).
- **The market assumptions** — cost of funds, LGD, operating cost, tax rate, capital ratio,
  hurdle — live in one place, `shared.config.MARKET`. They are not fitted to data; they are
  policy inputs, set and changed through change control (D9) like any other policy value.

The engine itself is tested as code: unit tests pin the waterfall and the rate solver.
This classification is a judgement, recorded here so that it can be challenged. A
validator working to a broader model definition (E-23 counts judgemental assumptions,
for instance) may reasonably inventory it as a low-tier model instead. What the
documentation must not do is leave it out of the inventory.

## Risk tiering

Tier 1 is the highest. The tier sets how much validation effort each component gets.

| Component | Tier | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Business Credit Score | 1 | Every other component consumes its output, so an error in it propagates into every decision the platform makes. |
| Loan Adjudication | 1 | It decides who gets credit: the largest financial and customer impact, and the one a declined applicant is owed reasons for. |
| Early Warning | 2 | It prioritises booked loans for human review; it does not change a credit decision by itself, and a miss is caught at the next review cycle. |
| Line Increase | 2 | It extends exposure, but only to the lower-risk half of the book and only where the incremental ROE clears the hurdle, so a miss costs a forgone offer or a small, bounded increase in exposure. |
| Pricing | tool | No estimated parameters (above). Its inputs are governed through the score (Tier 1) and the policy values in `shared.config.MARKET`. |

Two cautions a validator should apply to this table. The data are synthetic, so
"financial impact" here is the impact the platform *would* have on a real book of this
shape. And the tiers are the developer's proposal: under E-23 and SS1/23 the risk rating is
set by the institution's model risk function, not by the team that built the model.
